notable_absence.finding: The Prerequisites section is headed 'RBAC Privileges' and its body then requires a ROLE: 'Your client must have the **Query Use Sequential Scans** role on the keyspace'. So the page names a privilege heading and grants a role, and the registry - which promotes role:query-use-sequential-scans and a large privilege: namespace, and carries an explicit do-not-confuse warning about five unrelated things called 'role' - gets no requiresPrivilege relation from the page that looks most like it should supply one. This is the same privilege/role slippage the registry already flags, caught in the wild. Two further absences. (1) The page never says what a sequential scan actually DOES - no statement that it reads every document, or every key, in the collection; the reader is told it is slow ('the query takes one or more seconds'), best for small collections, and not high performance, but the mechanism is only ever named ('K/V range scan'), never described, and the K/V range scan link that would explain it does not exist. (2) No index-state, indexer-node-state or Active/Warmup/Paused vocabulary appears; the only 'state' on the page is "state": "completed", which belongs to the promoted query request status enum and to a REQUEST, not an index. A page whose whole subject is the absence of an index is a plausible place to say what state a keyspace with no index is in, and it says nothing.

cross_component_finding: Six things. (1) `"scanConsistency": "unbounded"` in the sample output, where index-replication.md in this same batch defines the four members as not_bounded, at_plus, request_plus and statement_plus. The monitoring surface spells the default value differently from the setting that produces it, and neither page mentions the other spelling - a reader filtering completed_requests on 'not_bounded' finds nothing. (2) 'Memory Only buckets' here, 'Memory-only buckets' on storage-modes.md, bucket:ephemeral-bucket in the registry: three spellings, two of them on adjacent pages of the same directory. (3) The two pages also read as contradictory on that bucket type - unsupported here, supported there - because one is about sequential scans and the other about index storage; true but hostile. (4) Namespace collision on the page's own subject: index:sequential-scan minted here versus n1ql:sequential-scan already in the corpus from server/8.0/n1ql/n1ql-manage/query-awr.json, and data:kv-range-scan here versus sdk:kv-range-scan in the corpus. Both collisions come from the same cause: a mechanism documented once as a query access path, once as an index topic, and once as an SDK API. (5) 'To query an index using sequential scan, run the query as usual' - the sentence that opens Use Sequential Scans describes querying an index in a section about there being no index, and the page's own next sentence says an index would be used instead. (6) The intro note says 'Query without Indexes is not available by default for paid service plans' and links to a section of the same page; the feature is called 'Query without Indexes' in that sentence, 'sequential scan' everywhere else, and 'Sequential Scans' in the section headings - the page's title and its subject have different names.
cross_product_finding: The gating story here is Capella-specific in a way that has no server/ analogue: a query feature that is ON for free clusters and OFF for paid ones, enabled not by a setting but by contacting support. The registry's promoted gatedByBillingPlan and requiresSupportPlan predicates exist for exactly this, but the plan concept the sentence needs - 'paid service plans' as a class, opposed to the free tier - is missing, so plan:paid-plan had to be minted next to four promoted plan ids. Second observation: the RBAC prerequisite is expressed with the promoted role:query-use-sequential-scans, a SERVER role id, on a Capella page that links to 'Manage Cluster Access Credentials' - so the Capella access model (cluster access credentials, capella-advanced-access-* privileges, of which the registry has thirty) and the server role model are both live in one three-line section, with no statement of how they relate. Third: `primaryScan.Seq` versus `primaryScan.GSI` is the only place in this batch where a monitoring field encodes the choice between an index and a non-index access path, and it does so with a token ('Seq') that appears nowhere else in the documentation, while the plan uses 'sequentialscan' and the prose uses 'sequential scan'. Three spellings, one mechanism, one page.
